Content:

We wish to design a hypothesis test at the [MATH: \alpha = 5\%] significance level to determine whether or not our suspicions are correct with the following null and alternative hypotheses:

Content:
- [MATH: H_0:\:\: p =\dfrac12]
- [MATH: H_1:\:\: p <\dfrac12]

Content:
Let the test statistic [MATH: X] equal the number of heads we get when the coin is tossed at random [MATH: 10] times in a row. Under the null hypothesis, our test statistic [MATH: X] can be modeled as the following binomial random variable:

[MATH: X\sim B\left(10,\dfrac12\right)]

The probability mass function [MATH: f(x)] of [MATH: X] is shown below.

Content:
The critical region is a set containing all possible [MATH: X]-values that are collectively unlikely under the null hypothesis and, therefore, cause the null hypothesis to be rejected. For left-tailed hypothesis tests like this, the critical regions lie to the left of the corresponding probability distribution.

Content:
Notice that getting either [MATH: 0,] [MATH: 1,] or [MATH: 2] heads out of [MATH: 10] coin tosses causes us to reject the null hypothesis, because

Content:

Content:
All of these values lie in the critical region. However, [MATH: X=3] does not lie in the critical region because

[MATH: P(X \leq 3) \approx 11.72\% > \alpha.]

Content:
Therefore, the critical region for this hypothesis test at the [MATH: 5\%] significance level is

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose we have a coin that we suspect is biased against landing on heads (i.e., the coin is less likely to land on heads than tails). We wish to design a hypothesis test at the [MATH: \alpha = 5\%] significance level to determine whether or not our suspicions are correct with the following null and alternative hypotheses:

Content:
- [MATH: H_0:\:\: p =\dfrac12]
- [MATH: H_1:\:\: p <\dfrac12]

Content:
Let the test statistic [MATH: X] equal the number of heads we get when the coin is tossed at random [MATH: 10] times in a row. Under the null hypothesis, our test statistic [MATH: X] can be modeled as the following binomial random variable:

Content:
[MATH: X\sim B\left(10,\dfrac12\right)]

Content:
The probability mass function [MATH: f(x)] of [MATH: X] is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/5b981e25330127c81a3670f95619611b]

Content:
The critical region is a set containing all possible [MATH: X]-values that are collectively unlikely under the null hypothesis and, therefore, cause the null hypothesis to be rejected. For left-tailed hypothesis tests like this, the critical regions lie to the left of the corresponding probability distribution.

Content:
Notice that getting either [MATH: 0,] [MATH: 1,] or [MATH: 2] heads out of [MATH: 10] coin tosses causes us to reject the null hypothesis, because

Content:
[MATH: P(X ≤ 0) ≈ 0.1% < α, P(X ≤ 1) ≈ 1.1% < α, P(X ≤ 2) ≈ 4.4% < α.]

Content:
All of these values lie in the critical region. However, [MATH: X=3] does not lie in the critical region because

Content:
[MATH: P(X \leq 3) \approx 11.72\% > \alpha.]

Content:
Therefore, the critical region for this hypothesis test at the [MATH: 5\%] significance level is

Content:
[MATH: X \in \{0, 1, {\color{red}{2}}\}.]

Content:
We can also write this as [MATH: X\leq 2.]

Content:
The value [MATH: X={\color{red}{2}}] is called the critical value. The critical value lies on the boundary between the critical region and the region where we do not reject [MATH: H_0.]

Content:
Finally, note that the critical region and critical value depend on our choice of [MATH: \alpha{:}]

Content:
- If we set [MATH: \alpha = 1\%,] for example, this reduces the likelihood of rejecting the null hypothesis.
- Consequently, the critical region is now [MATH: X\in \{{\color{red}{0}}\}] (or [MATH: X\leq 0]), and the critical value is [MATH: X={\color{red}{0}}.]
